propositions: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on.

Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.

The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.

However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.
In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.
Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.
He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.
“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000.
Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading blame for confrontations in Tigray amid international calls for restraint.
Their respective allies have the potential to catapult the conflict into a regional war.
Various sources have confirmed the presence of Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia .
An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in the northenmost state of Ethiopia, Tigray.
Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea have ramped up their war talk.
According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory.
In the letter, dated ‌Oct.

8, Ethiopian ‌Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia left "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea," in a post on X on October 7, Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Meskel had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war."

Two days later, he wrote in Tigrinya, a working language of Eritrea and the main language of Tigray, that "the sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law." adding "woe to those who touch it."
This comes as the regional conflict in Tigray has deteriorated rapidly in recent weeks.
Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation.
Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Egypt and Eritrea, causing the latter to sever diplomatic ties altogether.
On Monday, when Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years as Ethiopian prime minister , he stated that access to the sea was a priority.
The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side.

One is the Tsimdo movement, named after a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement."
"The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr.
Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW.
Eritrea has answered, in kind, a letter that Ethiopia sent to the United Nations Security Council on 9 October.
Addis Ababa’s letter described the entry of Eritrean forces deep into Ethiopian territory, by its account up to 60 kilometres, as a “blatant act of aggression”.
Asmara’s reply turned the charge back on Ethiopia, accusing it of preparing for a war that has been declared “for over three years now”.

The present escalation follows years of tension that set in as the previous conflict in Ethiopia’s northern region of Tigray drew to a close with the 2022 Pretoria agreement, a cessation of hostilities between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian government.
The agreement’s shaky implementation unfolded alongside the unravelling of the 2018 rapprochement between Addis Ababa and Isaias Afwerki’s regime in Asmara.
The dynamics now at play developed gradually in the years after the agreement.
Its terms required the TPLF to disband its armed wing and called for the restoration of federal authority and a new regional government in Tigray.
The TPLF split over the decision to sign, and its hardliner faction , dissatisfied with what it viewed as a surrender document, began taking steps to unpick the deal on the ground.
The hardliners sidelined the faction that backed Pretoria and gradually consolidated power in the region.
They also warmed to Eritrea, which had intervened against the group in the fighting, a sharp reversal of the regional order.
As the TPLF and Isaias grew closer, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara deteriorated, also for a mix of reasons.
Eritrea’s intervention in the Tigray conflict was brutal and, the Ethiopian prime minister told parliament in February this year, was a major cause of the rupture between the two capitals.
Ethiopia also began publicly stressing its aim of regaining the access to the sea it lost when Eritrea seceded more than three decades ago.
Asmara took that claim as an affront, even as the Ethiopian government ruled out the use of force in pursuing it.

The current fighting broke out in late September after a series of clashes that had fallen short of igniting a war, and this time it pitted the Ethiopian government against a coalition of seven rebel groups inside the country, spearheaded by the TPLF.

The coalition took shape from the alignment between the TPLF and Eritrea, which drew in groups such as the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) in Amhara, Tigray’s neighbouring region, and the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF), a smaller Afar group, as well as the Oromo Liberation Army in Oromia.
For Eritrea, the coalition marked the revival of a long-held strategy against its much larger and more powerful neighbour, proxy politics.

Isaias Afwerki, Eritrea’s strongman, has long fostered armed groups inside Ethiopia and across the Horn of Africa to offset Eritrea’s relative limitations and to project power and influence over its neighbours.

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Fears of intensifying conflict were growing in Saudi Arabia on Monday after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched multiple strikes on Riyadh’s airport over the weekend, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds.
“What is clear is we remain on a strong escalation ladder,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region.

More than 300 people were injured when the kingdom’s main international airport was attacked Saturday, marking a major escalation in the Houthi rebel group’s campaign against the world’s leading oil exporter and key U.S. ally in the region.
Among the victims were one American, as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese national.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia later said that an Indian national injured in Saturday’s attack had died.
Video capturing the Saturday attack showed a packed airport before the flash of an explosion sends people running for safety as debris falls on them.
The airport remained shut Monday.
The impact of the attacks were felt at the WPC Energy Congress in the Saudi capital Monday, with several top energy executives dropping off the event’s schedule.

The chief executives of Exxon Mobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which started Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organizers released early Monday, Reuters reported.
The energy giants did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News.

“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said, according to Reuters, as he opened Monday’s session of the gathering held just miles away from Riyadh airport.
But, he added, “our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”
He said the stepped-up fighting was serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious.”
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix,” he separately said.
“We come out of the ashes all the time and every time.”

Fighting on the ground in neighboring Yemen is also intensifying, with the Houthis expanding their operations along its Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb, a key shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 after the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

A period of relative calm following a 2022 ceasefire was shattered in July when the Houthis resumed attacks after accusing Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was attempting to land.

ANKARA — Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said on Monday that his government would submit the Makkah Agreement for Joint Defence to parliament in the coming days, as Türkiye condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed its support for the kingdom.
Erdoğan’s announcement comes after a series of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that have caused civilian casualties and widespread disruption to air travel.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes, describing the targeting of the airport as unacceptable and expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
The remarks reflect growing security coordination between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan under a defence agreement signed in Makkah on 7 August.
The pact states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries is to be treated as an attack against all, while providing for closer cooperation on defence and collective deterrence.
The three countries have already begun developing the agreement’s institutional framework.

At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on 5 October, their defence committee agreed to move towards implementing collective defence commitments and arranging the rapid deployment of agreed forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The committee also appointed a Pakistani former lieutenant general as the alliance’s first secretary-general.
Türkiye’s parliament has yet to ratify the agreement.
Its submission would bring the pact into the parliamentary process and could clarify how Ankara intends to fulfil its commitments.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Türkiye is assessing how it can assist Saudi Arabia, while ruling out sending troops or taking part in offensive operations.
Officials have indicated that Turkish support would focus on defensive and technical capabilities.
The diplomatic response follows a deadly attack on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday that Saudi authorities said killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
A further attack on Sunday killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others, according to Saudi reporting.
The Houthi movement has claimed responsibility for attacks on Saudi targets, including the airport.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt also issued a joint statement through the R4 grouping, holding the Houthis responsible for the airport attacks and calling for them to stop immediately.
The countries said they supported legitimate measures Saudi Arabia takes to protect its sovereignty and civilians.
The agreement is being developed amid renewed fighting in Yemen between Houthi forces and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government.

I want to help 12 Oct 2026 | Advocacy , Joint Statement , News The Coalition for the International Criminal Court (CICC), the more than 120 undersigned organisations from over 60 countries representing all regions, and dozens of legal experts, human rights defenders and members of the European Parliament, condemn unequivocally and in the strongest terms the decision by co the United States (US) to impose unlawful sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC).

This unprecedented measure represents a direct attack against the rule of law, the independence of the Court and international justice, ultimately undermining the rights of millions of victims and survivors of mass atrocities worldwide.
The ICC has shown remarkable resilience in steadfastly discharging its mandate in the face of escalating attacks.
Now, States Parties must match this commitment by defending the Court they themselves established and protecting those who cooperate with it.
Condemnations alone are not enough; coordinated action is urgently needed to protect the Court’s ability to function.
On 9 October 2026, the US announced the imposition of sanctions against the ICC as an institution under Executive Order 14203 .

These sanctions mark the gravest escalation in the sustained campaign carried out by the US with the declared aim of dismantling the ICC “brick by brick” for having investigated crimes allegedly committed on the territory of a State Party by US nationals or their allies, in particular Israeli nationals .
Under the Rome Statute, the Court may exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed on the territory of a State Party, irrespective of the nationality of the alleged perpetrator.

Since February 2025, the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on the former ICC Prosecutor, Karim Khan ; both Deputy Prosecutors ; the ICC President and eight other judges; a staff member and judicial candidate ; a UN Special Rapporteur ; and three Palestinian human rights organisations .
These measures aim to undermine the Rome Statute system as a whole and to prevent the investigation and prosecution of international crimes.

Executive Order 14203 prohibits US persons from providing material support or services to designated persons and entities, including financial services, and exposes non-US persons to the risk of secondary sanctions for engaging in conduct prohibited under the Executive Order.
US persons who violate it may face criminal penalties of up to 20 years’ imprisonment and fines of up to 1 million USD, as well as civil penalties.
Although the Executive Order contains a six-month wind-down period and exemptions for certain services, significant risks remain.

Given the global reliance on the US financial and IT systems, even non-US service providers, including banks, may stop rendering their services to the ICC out of fear of penalties or reprisals from the US Treasury.
This could impact the Court’s ability to maintain a bank account, receive financial contributions from States Parties, make payments, pay staff and maintain essential operations.
The Netherlands, as the host country, and all States Parties are responsible for ensuring the ICC can maintain access to services critical to its operations.
The Court must be able to continue to carry out its core functions, including investigating alleged crimes; holding hearings; protecting victims and witnesses; and providing legal aid services.

Rumours have been circulating for weeks about the United States imposing tougher sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), because of what US President Donald Trump sees as unfair targeting of Americans and Israelis for prosecution.
These sanctions finally came into effect on October 9 - the same day South African jurist Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her contribution to international law.
The motivations behind these two diametrically opposing moves speak to the fragility of international law.

They also highlight that ICC member states - including Australia, Japan, EU states and Canada - might need to decide between Trump's program to dismantle the ICC " brick by brick " and their own commitments to international justice.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The US has never been a strong supporter of the ICC.
While it took part in negotiations that created the court's founding treaty in 1998, it did so partly to ensure the crime of aggression remained off the court's remit for decades.
Former President Bill Clinton did sign the Rome Statute in 1998, but it was never ratified.
Bush removed this possibility in 2002.
Congress went further later the same year by passing the American Servicemembers' Protection Act (ASPA) (aka "the Hague invasion act").
The concern here was to ensure no US citizen could fall under the ICC's jurisdiction.
The US has since entered into many bilateral agreements, including with ICC member states, to ensure US nationals are not handed over to The Hague.
Afghanistan accepted the ICC's jurisdiction in 2003.
In 2017, prosecutor Fatou Bensouda called for a full investigation that included allegations of CIA torture in "black sites" in Poland, Romania and Lithuania.
The appeals chamber confirmed this in March 2020.
Consequently, the US imposed "smart sanctions" on two ICC officials - including Bensouda - in September 2020.
It has also targeted the UN's expert on the Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese .
This prevented her from all financial dealings or travel to the US.
In April 2021, with Joe Biden was in office, the sanctions were revoked.
The sanctions targeting the ICC, which prosecutes humanitarian crimes, are the latest move by the US against the court.

The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after one of its former judges was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in what the Nobel committee said was, in part, a show of support for institutions under attack.
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also in The Hague, was announced winner of the prize on Friday.
Nobel Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice,” the committee said.
The US move follows sanctions it has already imposed this year on judges and other personnel at the ICC.

On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the latest set of US sanctions targeting the ICC, this time focusing on the court itself, which was established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” he said in a video shared on social media.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC has gone beyond its remit by pursuing non-member countries.

In 2024, the Trump administration condemned the court when it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for suspected war crimes in Gaza.
It also previously opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan.
The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction.
However, abuses committed by citizens of non-statute states in ICC territories or countries can still be prosecuted.

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement, adding that if the US allies failed to “rein in the court”, the US would “continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”.
These sanctions are just the latest in the US’s campaign against the ICC.

Previous measures have targeted dozens of ICC judges and prosecutors , the UN special rapporteur for Palestine, Francesca Albanese, and Palestinian rights groups which have provided evidence of war crimes committed by Israel to the court.

Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they intend to disrupt an Arab-operated and United States-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran.

With the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

This strategic waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas flowed before the war, has been largely closed to shipping following Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
But the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid an energy crisis.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei responded on Sunday night, saying the shuttle system is now an explicit target for Tehran.
Rezaei claimed that the US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers.
He claimed Iran had been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.
“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.
This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.
Rezaei appeared to give the impression that Iran wants to have lasting authority over Hormuz, and promised a harsh response if Iran’s energy and civilian infrastructure were attacked again.
His threats appeared aimed at Arab regional states, with a warning that digital infrastructure could be targeted.
Rezaei threatened US-linked cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the UAE and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Rezaei also accused Saudi Arabia of helping the US move oil around Iran’s restrictions.
But he did not threaten a direct attack against Riyadh – which is currently being targeted by Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis.
In early September, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened tankers at ports and anchorages in Kuwait and Bahrain, citing US attacks on Iranian tankers .
It accused both countries of complicity through hosting US armed forces.
Iran has claimed the US accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war.

European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defense company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport.
If Russia decides to attack NATO, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander U.S.

The NATO commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to "resolve misunderstandings."

The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia.

It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran .

Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said.

NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it.

The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan.
Asked whether the plan factored in a scenario where the U.S. was engaged elsewhere, Grynkewich said: “It absolutely does account for that, and in fact, it must.”

After a lengthy process marked by controversy and opposition, Bangladesh today signed a 15-year concession agreement with UAE-based DP World to operate and maintain the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its overflow container yard at Chattogram port.
The agreement was signed at the Chattogram Port Authority (CPA) headquarters this afternoon.
CPA Chairman Rear Admiral S M Moniruzzaman and Essa Kazim, chairman of DP World, signed the agreement on behalf of their respective sides.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, served as the transaction adviser for the deal.
Local company Saif Powertec Ltd had been operating the terminal for years.
After its contract expired on July 6 last year, Chittagong Dry Dock Ltd, a Bangladesh Navy-run company, took over its operation.
The process to appoint an international operator for the NCT began in 2019.
In March 2023, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs gave in-principle approval to appoint an international private operator under a public-private partnership framework.
The interim government later revived the initiative and selected DP World for the project.
The process, however, stalled amid strong opposition and a workers' strike earlier this year.
The current government subsequently resumed negotiations over the proposed concession.
Built in 2007 at a cost of around Tk 2,000 crore, the NCT has five jetties and 14 of the Chattogram port's 18 quay-side gantry cranes.
More than 40 percent of the port's container handling takes place through the terminal.
The move to hand over the NCT to a foreign operator has faced opposition from the Chattogram Port Protection Committee.
On October 5, the committee staged a sit-in in front of the port headquarters and warned of shutting down port operations if the deal with a foreign operator was finalised.
The government has said the agreement will help reduce vessel turnaround time and container dwell time, lowering logistics costs for importers and exporters.
It expects sectors such as readymade garments, agricultural products, processed goods and light engineering to benefit from improved port efficiency.

Adviser to the Prime Minister on Finance and Planning Prof Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir today (12 October) said Bangladesh has reached broad policy alignment with the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on key economic reforms aimed at restoring stability, strengthening discipline in the banking sector, increasing tax revenue and creating employment.

"The government is pursuing a comprehensive economic recovery and reconstruction strategy, with greater domestic and foreign investment, reopening closed factories, expanding social protection and addressing rising energy costs among its major priorities," he said.
The adviser made the remarks while speaking to journalists ahead of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Thailand, said a press release.
Titumir said the government had a politically mandated roadmap to recover, restore and rapidly rebuild the economy to put the country on a path to prosperity.
The plan has been outlined in a five-year economic strategy, with several fundamental priorities aligning with the reform proposals of the World Bank and the IMF, he added.

"The people want discipline in the financial sector, higher tax collection relative to GDP, increased spending on social protection and employment generation through industrialisation," he said, adding that reopening closed factories was also a public expectation.
The adviser said alignment between the government's reform priorities and those of multilateral development partners would facilitate implementation and improve the prospects for sustainable reforms.
However, he emphasised that the political government would retain ownership of the reform agenda and responsibility for its implementation.

Titumir said the government had discussed with the World Bank the additional financial pressure on the energy sector arising from the conflict in the Middle East, which began on 28 February, and its impact on ordinary people.
He said the government had refrained from fully adjusting domestic energy prices to international market levels to limit the burden on consumers.
Referring to the World Bank's recent report, he said poverty had increased during the previous government's tenure.
The present government is planning to support poor households through programmes such as the Family Card, he added.
According to assessments by independent research institutions, such initiatives could potentially reduce the poverty rate by around five percentage points over five years, he said.
The government has also highlighted the need for financing to strengthen climate resilience, expand renewable energy and develop essential infrastructure.
Titumir identified restoring discipline in the financial sector as one of the major challenges to economic recovery.
He said ordinary citizens were now bearing the consequences of irregularities and lending-related disorder in the banking sector during the previous administration.

Restoring confidence in banks and rehabilitating the weakened financial system would require refinancing support, he said, adding that discussions were underway with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and other institutions on the issue.
Without stability in the banking sector, it would be difficult to achieve the targets for higher investment and employment, he continued.

Olivia Chow says she’ll create a citywide universal student nutrition program if re-elected mayor, a policy her chief rival says is well-meaning but unfunded and something experts say Toronto can’t do alone.
Chow made the campaign pledge earlier this week to expand the city’s school food program, which currently provides midday snacks, to also cover lunch.
The system serves about 330,000 students every day, with the city contributing $32 million this year.
The mayor pitched the plan as a key affordability measure in her re-election bid, saying it will help the average family save $1,800 a year.
But she could not say how much the expansion would cost taxpayers — only that it will be phased in by 2030 and done in conjunction with other levels of government and private donors.
“You know, when a child is hungry in school, they cannot focus,” Chow said at a debate in Scarborough this week.
“We have to do lunches because it will save parents a whole lot of money.”

Brad Bradford, Chow’s main challenger in the race, said while he supports the idea, the mayor has not said how the city will pay for it.
“What concerns me about the proposal in front of us today about lunch programs is, of course, there is no national program for that. There is no provincial program for that,” he said.
Chow shot back that she can bring the other governments onside.
“What matters is taking the leadership, having the vision, to say this is what we need, and having the ambition and the courage to say that no kids should be hungry in school,” Chow said.
Right now, the city’s student food program is funded by all three levels of government and private donors and grants.
According to a Toronto Public Health presentation from last year, in 2024-2025, the city received $4.7 million in federal funding and $8.5 million in provincial funding for school food programs.
That left the city as the largest funding source at $21.9 million, which was upped to $32 million in the 2026 budget.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first budget includes plans to give the program permanent funding of $216.6 million.
(Ben Nelms/CBC) Neither the federal government or province could say Friday if they are committed to funding an expansion of Toronto's plan to a universal program.
In 2024, the federal government announced it would spend $1 billion over five years to work with provinces on implementing a school food program.

Photo: Group photo of Wasauksing Manoomin Youth and Survey Tour on Wasauksing August 2026 Wasauksing First Nation partnered with the Anishinabek/Ontario Fisheries Resource Centre (A/OFRC) this summer to assess the health and potential of manoomin (wild rice) habitats in the community.
Close up shot of manoomin (wild rice).
Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The aim of the project is to follow the community’s lead in restoring a food source that is central to Anishinaabe culture, food sovereignty and identity.

In spring 2026, Wasauksing submitted a proposal to A/OFRC to support the revival of manoomin beds through scientific expertise and state-of-the-art tools while remaining grounded in the community’s own local knowledge.

For Wasauksing’s Lands and Resources Office, success means more than ecological recovery — it also means “restoring personal and community well-being and self-determination; being able to manage and harvest traditional foods, strengthening our Nation’s food sovereignty.”
The project aims to support the reclamation of cultural practices and traditional knowledge surrounding manoomin, while deepening community connection to land, water, and cultural identity.
Through A/OFRC, Wasauksing has visited communities like Alderville to learn from Elders like Jeff Beaver, whose community has been running a wild rice reintroduction project since the 1990s.

Gabrielle Perugini, A/OFRC’s lead fisheries biologist, said much of what they have learned as an organization and what makes these sort of restoration projects possible comes from knowledge keepers like Jeff Beaver from Alderville First Nation.

Youth from the community spent a week alongside the A/OFRC team exploring local waters, learning the history of manoomin in their territory and getting hands-on experience with the monitoring and surveying of identified sites.
“There were lots of smiles and laughing, lots of knowledge transfer and storytelling while we were out in the canoes checking in on the sites,” said Perugini.
Monitoring turbidity and water quality at manoomin sites.
Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The fieldwork encouraged the youth to be part of the restoration efforts by learning how to use equipment to measure water quality at potential manoomin sites.
They measured and recorded pH, turbidity, sediment composition, and water levels.

They also learned to identify and document optimal growing conditions: slow-moving, clear water; lakes with inflow and outflow; depths between 0.5 and three feet; minimal water level fluctuations; and silty sediment.
“I think it’s important not only from the stewardship side of things, but crucial for their spiritual connection to the land,” Perugini said of the youth’s involvement.

“If you get the youth involved, they start to develop a personal relationship with the manoomin, and having some personal stake in the matter fuels their stewardship. People will protect what they love and value. The hope is that it spreads to more youth and, in the blink of an eye, you have manoomin guardians at the ready.”
Gabrielle Perugini from A/OFRC teaching youth how to take soil samples.
Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland While it is too early for a final report — A/OFRC still needs to compile and analyze the data — the early assessments were encouraging.

When Aidan Traverse returned to Fisher River Cree Nation following a hunting trip on Friday, he brought more than 500 kilograms of fresh moose meat with him.

Traverse, 18, is one of eight students who travelled nearly 400 kilometres to Moose Mountain Provincial Park in southeast Saskatchewan on Oct. 5, as part of a land-based education program offered through Fisher River High School.
The group harvested four bull moose over the course of the five-day hunting trip, returning triumphant with the meat packed into a cooler trailer.
It was Traverse's first time hunting big game, and he plans to share the harvest with the community in Fisher River, a First Nation in Manitoba's Interlake, about 175 kilometres north of Winnipeg.
"You feel honoured to be out there," said Traverse, who hunted with his elders in mind.
"I have my granny — she's always been wanting moose meat, and then my grandmother-in-law, she's been asking me too."

Traverse and other Grade 11 and 12 students are benefitting from a renewed focus on land-based learning in Fisher River, where leaders believe academic success should prioritize emotional, spiritual and cultural health — not just letter grades.
He met with CBC News on Oct. 2, as preparations for the hunting trip were underway.

The haul included two large prospector tents, a pair of 113-litre coolers, four propane tanks and 90 litres of fuel, among other items.
"This is only half of the stuff," Amos, 25, said with a laugh.
This year marks the second time Amos has helped lead students on a guided hunt at Moose Mountain.
The group took down multiple moose and other game last year and later hosted a community feast for more than 300 people.

"There was a spark in the kids after," Amos said.

The government has transferred the unused machinery from the Sonali Bag project to Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University (MBSTU) to prevent public assets from deteriorating and support further research into jute-based products and technologies.
A memorandum of understanding was signed on October 8 among the Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation (BJMC), the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust and the university.
State Minister for Textiles and Jute Shariful Alam handed over the machinery to the university’s vice-chancellor.
The move comes after the much-anticipated Sonali Bag -- a biodegradable alternative to plastic, made from jute cellulose -- failed to become commercially viable.
According to a BJMC statement sent to The Daily Star, the Tk 100 crore project was scrapped on April 29, 2025, following a technical committee’s recommendation.
The 11-member committee found that producing five tonnes of Sonali bags required 40 tonnes of chemicals, raising environmental concerns.
Each bag would need to sell for Tk 25-40 to cover production costs, making it commercially unviable, the statement said.
Talking to The Daily Star, Shariful Alam said the government is working with the environment ministry and other institutions to develop environmentally friendly alternatives to polythene bags.
Although the project had made technological progress, production costs could not be reduced to commercially acceptable levels, he said.
The state minister said the machinery will support research into jute cellulose, eco-friendly products and new technologies.
Private researchers will also be able to access the facilities, while the ministry may use them for research and training.
Shariful Alam said reusable jute bags could offer long-term savings despite their higher initial cost.
Dr Mubarak Ahmed Khan, who invented the Sonali Bag in 2016, said the project stalled because the government did not provide the necessary funding.
He subsequently left the project, he said.
Questioning the production-cost estimate, Khan said a feasibility study put the cost at Tk 500 per kilogramme, but he did not know how the figure had been calculated.
He argued that costs would fall as production increased and said he had presented his own calculations to officials.
Several local and foreign companies have since expressed interest in the technology, he said.

Syrian Security Forces Step Up anti-ISIS Operations, Pursue Former Regime Loyalists Syrian security forces have intensified operations against ISIS cells following a deadly September bus attack near Masyaf in central Syria, while separately pursuing former regime operatives accused of crimes against civilians.
Within a week, authorities announced the dismantling of an ISIS cell in Homs province, following the arrest of the group’s alleged military commander there.
Seven former regime suspects were also detained as part of transitional justice efforts.

The Internal Security Forces announced that raids in the Houla area of northern Homs, conducted with the General Intelligence Directorate, had dismantled an ISIS-linked cell and foiled planned attacks on places of worship and security patrols.
Two suspects were arrested and two explosive devices were seized.
Preliminary investigations indicated that the detainees had received and transported explosives and monitored potential targets as part of plans to incite unrest and undermine security.
One suspect was caught attempting to plant an explosive device on a railway track, authorities reported.
Investigations are continuing to identify other cell members and their connections.
The operation followed the arrest about three days earlier of Khaled Raed Bayrouni, known as Abu Hassan Doshka, in Hujayra, near Damascus.
The Interior Ministry described him as ISIS’s operational arm in Homs and the group’s overall military commander in its so-called Homs province.
Bayrouni is accused of planning and overseeing bombings and sectarian attacks, including an explosion at an Alawite mosque in Homs that killed eight people in late 2025.
Authorities also launched raids and arrests following a Sept. 27 attack on a bus transporting workers near the Masyaf bypass bridge, on the road linking Masyaf and Homs, that killed seven civilians.

PHNOM PENH — In Cambodia’s Koh Sdach archipelago, where turquoise waters hide mounting environmental pressures from overfishing and plastic waste to climate change, one local leader has turned grassroots action into a model for marine conservation.

Koh Sdach commune deputy chief Sorn Srenh, a marine advocate who studied fishery science at the Royal University of Agriculture in Phnom Penh, stands at the intersection of science, policy, and community advocacy.
For years, the 38-year-old has worked relentlessly with the fishing community to protect their livelihoods while pushing for sustainable practices that safeguard marine biodiversity.

His efforts, ranging from organizing community capacity to lobbying for stronger local enforcement of fishing regulations, have made him a trusted voice among villagers and a rare example of commune-level leadership driving tangible environmental change.

For years, Srenh has also been working with the Cambodian government’s Fisheries Administration and the UK-based NGO Fauna & Flora to help establish Koh Sdach’s community fisheries management area, known as a Marine Fisheries Management Area (MFMA).

In a phone interview with Mongabay, Srenh shared his vision for community-led conservation, the challenges of balancing economic survival with ecological stewardship, and why protecting Cambodia’s seas matters far beyond its shores.
Mongabay: Can you describe your journey from studying fishery science to becoming a grassroots conservation leader in Koh Sdach?
What encourages you to protect marine ecosystems?
Sorn Srenh: I love fisheries management because of a formative experience in the Koh Sdach archipelago.

When an NGO launched a marine conservation initiative and invited me to work with them, watching their activities — scuba diving, underwater photography, and community capacity building to encourage local participation in biodiversity conservation — captivated me and sparked my curiosity about marine ecosystems.
That experience motivated me to explore the sea’s ecosystem more deeply and follow my curiosity to learn more.
Mongabay: Why are marine resources so important for families in Koh Sdach?
Are there specific practices or agreements you’ve established that helped reduce overfishing or habitat damage?
Sorn Srenh: Community livelihoods in this archipelago highly depend on fishery resources, as fishing is their main source of income, on top of the tourism sector.
For long-term sustainability, we have community fishing areas [designated zones where local fishers are allowed to manage and harvest sea resources] to be protected across this archipelago.
Marine species such as sea turtles, coral reefs, and seagrass meadows are highly vulnerable to overfishing, yet they play a critical role in maintaining healthy marine ecosystems.
To safeguard these species, I have been working relentlessly with community members, local partners, and the government’s fisheries department to strengthen community-based conservation efforts.

Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear.
His tools are still there, but the customers are not.
Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted.
The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts.
For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras.
He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal.
Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place.
Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair.
Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s.
Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh.

“Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842.
“They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added.
Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike.
“Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained.
“The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.”
Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand.
“In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said.
“But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.”

In Mozambique , freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014 , a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique .

However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience.
In music, for example, this contradiction is clear.
Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo .

More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s , but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party.
Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces.
Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “ O ciclo da Censura ” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?”
This is not just a provocative artistic comment.
It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences.
Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically.

While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum , digital platforms for monitoring local governance , cultural associations, and artistic initiatives.
This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces.
However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order.
One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools .

JAKARTA — Indonesia says it no longer needs to expand rice cultivation into forest areas, but it has yet to explain what the announcement means for large-scale food and energy projects already underway in Papua and Kalimantan.

Presidential Special Envoy for Climate and Energy Hashim Djojohadikusumo said Oct. 6 that Indonesia had achieved rice self-sufficiency three years ahead of schedule and no longer needed the previously announced 2 million hectares (4.9 million acres) for food production.
“The government sees no further need for expanding rice cultivation areas in the so-called forest areas and forest zones that were announced a few years ago,” Hashim said in Jakarta.
At the same event, President’s Special Envoy for Multilateralism and International Trade Mari Pangestu said future food and biofuel production would instead be directed toward degraded land.

The announcement appears to mark a shift from a government push that environmentalists have described as one of the world’s largest deforestation projects , involving vast rice and sugarcane plantations in southern Papua.

But less than two weeks before Hashim’s announcement, the Ministry of Forestry designated about 5.67 million hectares (14 million acres) of forest through its 2026 Forest Utilization Direction Map, or PAPH, as areas that could be proposed for forest-utilization permits, including for food security and energy, as well as forest rehabilitation.

“This means there is an inconsistency between the statements issued by public officials,” Indonesian Forum for the Environment (Walhi) campaigner for essential ecosystems Musdalifah Jamal told Mongabay by phone.
“This contradiction shows us that the government has not yet abandoned a development paradigm that places forest areas as spaces to fulfill food and energy needs.”
The forestry ministry has welcomed the direction of Hashim’s announcement but has not said whether it changes existing policies or projects.

“A distinction needs to be made between new expansion plans that require the clearing of forest areas, activities that are already under way, and increasing production on agricultural land that is already available,” ministry spokesperson Ristianto Pribadi said, as quoted by The Straits Times .
“Therefore, we cannot yet say that all activities in the two regions will automatically stop, nor confirm when they will stop,” he said, referring to South Papua and Central Kalimantan.
Environmental groups say the announcement must therefore be followed by changes to policies that have facilitated forest conversion.

“At face value, the statements from Pak Hashim and Ibu Mari Pangestu said the Government of Indonesia would no longer pursue deforestation for food or energy crops,” Mighty Earth founder and CEO Glenn Hurowitz told Mongabay.
“In order for these positive statements to have impact, they have to be implemented, including by changes in decrees and other policies.”
Nadia Hadad, executive director of NGO MADANI Berkelanjutan, said the government also needs to align its food, energy, forestry and fiscal policies with the new commitment.
“Climate commitments are ultimately not measured by how many statements are made, but by whether policies and state money move in the same direction,” she said in a press release.

Franky Samperante, director of the Pusaka Foundation, which works with Indigenous peoples in Papua, said officials often express commitments to sustainable development and forest protection that have yet to be translated into concrete policies and actions.

Draft national strategy accepts the wily invasive species can’t be eradicated but outlines steps to protect native animals most at risk They dart across playgrounds on dainty paws, sneak into back yard coops to eat suburban chickens and kill more than a million native animals every day.

The European red fox – a wily invasive species – is “one of the most impactful threats” for native mammals, says Sarah Legge, a professor at Charles Darwin University and author of a new draft plan to curb their predation.

“Australia has the worst record of mammal extinctions of any country in the world – around 40 species – and the overwhelming cause for those extinctions has been predation by foxes and cats,” Legge says.
If the federal environment department moves ahead with the plan, Australia would have its first updated national effort to halt the impact of foxes on native wildlife in nearly two decades.
Legge says there have been dramatic advancements in understanding how to combat foxes since the last plan was released in 2008.
Populations are hard to gauge, but estimates put the number about 1.7 million spread across the country , from central Queensland down through New South Wales to Victoria and South Australia.
Populations are also thriving in Western Australia.
All those foxes are hungry, with studies estimating foxes kill upwards of 367 million native mammals, 111 million birds, 88 million reptiles and “countless” invertebrates and frogs each year.
The draft plan acknowledges that foxes are far too numerous to eradicate but steps can be taken to protect the species most at risk.
These include increased funding for safe havens such as fox-free islands and fenced, predator-proof zones .
The plan also calls for collaboration and “legislative harmony” between states and the federal government.
“I’m not pretending that we can get rid of foxes from across the continent any time soon,” Legge says.
“But we can definitely stop native wildlife population loss and extinction.”
Rob Brewster, the rewilding manager at the Invasive Species Council, says ecologists have spent the past 18 years learning everything they can about foxes and the species they hunt.

A dozen key species have been identified as extremely susceptible to fox predation, including the critically endangered Gilbert’s potoroo; the endangered eastern quoll; endangered eastern barred and western barred bandicoots; and species of bettongs, hare-wallabies and the Tasmanian pademelon.
Seven species of freshwater turtles are on the list, too.
Researchers have said for nearly a decade that without urgent action, all face the threat of extinction.
“It’s not climate change, it’s not habitat loss, those things are all bad … but the key driver of these extinctions is foxes and cats,” Brewster says.

Discovery suggests raw ingredients for life are common in the dusty discs out of which planets are born.
The materials that form the building blocks of life on Earth have been found in distant planet-forming discs that are the same size as the Solar System.
Our Solar System formed from a dusty ring of cosmic material circling the Sun , when our host star was still just a stellar newborn.
This ring - known as a protoplanetary disk - contained solid materials that coalesced through gravity over time, eventually growing into the the planets orbiting the Sun that we see today.

Studying other young stars and their protoplanetary discs enables astronomers to analyse the conditions that may have led to the formation of of our own Solar System, and perhaps even the development of life on Earth.
Dr John Ilee is an astrophysicist studying star and planet formation at the University of Leeds.

Using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, he and his colleagues have identified organic molecules in protoplanetary discs around young stars, which could point to the building blocks required for the development of organic life.
These discs are located between about 300 to 500 lightyears from Earth, so we are actually seeing the discs as they appeared 300 to 500 years ago.
The regions in which these discs exist are some of the closest star-forming regions to our Solar System, which means we can get an excellent view of them.
Compared to previous instruments, ALMA has hugely increased our observational capability.
It combines extremely high sensitivity with a high spatial resolution.
This means we can detect faint emission on small scales, which was essential for our study.
We searched for the unique ‘fingerprints’ of these molecules in the ALMA data, which were very faint, but thanks to the data’s exceptional quality we were able to detect their emission.

These molecules have been detected in protoplanetary discs before, but the fact that we’ve been able to get such improved observations means the abundance of these molecules is much higher than previously thought.
Additionally, they’re located in the ‘inner’ disc regions, within about 50 astronomical units, which is approximately the same scale as our Solar System.
This means we are finding significant amounts of prebiotic materials (which form the building blocks of life) on similar scales to a planetary system like our own.
The findings suggest that the chemical composition of discs that appear to be forming planets is similar to the composition of our own Solar System.
However, we don’t know if this is required to form planets.

Astronomers investigating mysterious flashes of X-rays believe that these blasts could stem from collisions between neutron stars, the events that forge elements like gold, silver, and platinum.
The event designated EP250704a, was first seen on July 4, 2025, as a blast of gamma rays lasting half a second followed by a bright X-ray emission lasting 10 minutes.

After receiving an alert from the joint European-Chinese Einstein probe that witnessed the blast, a team of astronomers started to hunt for its cause by studying the aftermath of the explosion using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Very Large Array (VLA), and other telescopes.
According to astronomer Niccolò Passaleva who led the observations of the X-ray flash with the VLT, this cosmic outburst was unlike any scientists had seen before.
"This is the longest-lasting prompt X-ray flash ever observed from a neutron star merger," Passaleva said in a statement .

Science · Not yet confirmed elsewhere 1 publisher · 2 min read · Published Oct 10, 2026, 1:30 AM PDT Astronomers attribute EP250704a, a half-second gamma-ray burst followed by 10 minutes of X-rays, to two neutron stars colliding.
The event gives them a test case for the hundreds of X-ray flashes Einstein Probe has logged since its 2024 launch, some of them still unexplained.
The X-ray emission lasted about 1,200 times as long as the gamma-ray spike before it [16] .
Neutron-star mergers, the collisions space.com credits with forging gold, silver and platinum [12] , have long been associated with gamma-ray flashes that fade within two seconds [5] .
Some new research suggests that mergers can also show up as X-ray blasts lasting minutes [6] .
The long X-rays caught the team's attention early.
"When I saw the X-ray data from this new event, I realized something was up," said Eleonora Troja, a member of the Einstein Probe European collaboration [15] .
The team's explanation for the extra minutes is a magnetar.
According to space.com, the researchers think at least one was involved in the merger [9] .
A collapsing stellar core can spin the neutron star it leaves behind up to more than 700 rotations a second [13] .
The collapse also squeezes the magnetic field lines together, which strengthens the field.
A core that starts out strongly magnetised can end as a magnetar, the object with the strongest magnetic field in the universe [13] .
Troja framed the idea as a conditional.
"If the remnant of the collision is a magnetar, it could keep bursting for longer," she said.
"Magnetars are rapidly spinning neutron stars with huge magnetic fields. When they dump their magnetic power into the surroundings, they can make any explosion brighter and longer-lasting."
[10] We treat the merger as the team's best current interpretation.
In space.com's account, the case rests on ruling out a supernova [8] .
The account does not describe any positive sign of a merger in the VLT or VLA data, such as the kilonova light that marks these collisions [5] .

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: A new species of ancient crocodile relative that lived around 170 million years ago has been discovered by scientists at the University of Portsmouth and Hassan II University of Casablanca, Morocco.
Unlike most crocodiles, this animal had a long, narrow snout filled with exceptionally thin, needlelike teeth.
The teeth were so slender that they are unlike those of any known close relative.
The animal, named Ctenosuchus tenuidens, belonged to a group of marine and freshwater reptiles known as thalattosuchians, which lived during the age of the dinosaurs.
The fossils were found in rocks that formed in ancient rivers and lakes in what is now the Atlas Mountains of southeastern Morocco.
Hamzah Imran from the University of Portsmouth's School of the Environment and Life Sciences is lead author of the research published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology .

He said, "We noticed these little black circles on either side of the long bone in the middle of one of the fossils, so we put it under a microscope. "We carefully scratched around one of the black circles with a scalpel, and as we uncovered more of it, it became longer and longer.
That's when we realized these little black circles were actually incredibly thin teeth.
By studying the fossil teeth under powerful microscopes and examining their internal structure, Imran and his colleagues found that the teeth had specialized ridges and were closely spaced.
These features suggest that Ctenosuchus had a very unusual diet.
Rather than hunting large prey, it likely fed on very small fish, crustaceans such as fairy shrimp and other small aquatic creatures.

Imran said, "The teeth are so fine that we don't think it was catching normal prey. If it caught a big fish, and the fish wriggled, those delicate teeth would get smashed. We think the animal was probably eating soft prey like shrimp, worms and tiny fish, so nothing that would break its teeth. "These feeding habits make this particular species very different from other long-snouted crocodiles, so it really is quite an exciting discovery!" The research helps scientists better understand the diversity and ecology of ancient crocodile relatives that lived in the southern supercontinent Gondwana, which included modern-day Africa. It also shows that different groups of prehistoric animals evolved similar feeding adaptations independently. The teeth of Ctenosuchus resemble those seen in some ancient aquatic reptiles called mesosaurs and even certain long-snouted pterosaurs that lived millions of years later. In fact, the jaws and teeth of Ctenosuchus have many similarities with the jaws of some Jurassic pterosaurs such as Gnathosaurus and Ctenochasma that scientists believe were filter feeders. Overall, the fossils reveal that Jurassic crocodile relatives occupied a wider range of habitats and feeding roles than previously realized, highlighting the rich prehistoric ecosystems that once existed in Morocco. Imran added, "It just shows there is much more out there that needs to be explored.

A single high dose of psilocybin in people who had never taken a psychedelic was followed by improvements in well-being, psychological insight, and cognitive flexibility a month later, and participants whose brain activity became more irregular during the experience tended to show the largest well-being gains.
Lasting changes in brain function, however, were largely absent, though the researchers detected possible changes in the brain’s white matter.
The findings were published in Nature Communications .
Psilocybin is the active psychedelic compound found in “magic mushrooms.”
It works primarily by stimulating a specific type of serotonin receptor in the brain.
Some scientists have proposed that this chemical action scrambles normal brain activity into a more flexible, highly disordered state.

For instance, a 2014 theoretical paper by Robin Carhart-Harris, the senior author of the new study, introduced the “entropic brain” hypothesis, suggesting that psychedelics expand conscious experience by making brain signals more unpredictable.
Researchers have suspected that this temporary disruption might lead to lasting benefits.
Along these lines, a 2021 open-label study of 24 people with depression found that psilocybin improved cognitive flexibility for at least a month.
Cognitive flexibility is a person’s ability to successfully adapt their thinking and switch between different rules or concepts.
Scientists then began tracking healthy volunteers for weeks after a single dose to see whether these acute disruptions leave enduring functional or physical marks on the brain.

For example, a small 2020 study of 12 healthy volunteers found that some changes in mood and resting brain connectivity were still detectable a month after a single high dose, although others had faded.

Similarly, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that psilocybin temporarily scrambled brain network connections, with most changes fading within weeks but some, such as reduced connectivity between the hippocampus and a network involved in self-reflection, persisting.

Building on this progression, the current research, led by Taylor Lyons of the Centre for Psychedelic Research at Imperial College London, sought to capture a comprehensive picture of what happens in the brain of someone taking a psychedelic for the very first time.
The researchers aimed to connect the immediate, disorganized brain state during a trip to the psychological benefits reported weeks later.
They also wanted to test whether a single high dose of psilocybin physically alters the structure of the brain’s white matter.
The study involved 28 healthy adults, averaging 41 years old, who had never taken a psychedelic drug before.

Each participant received two oral doses of psilocybin one month apart, always in the same order: first a 1-milligram dose, too low to produce noticeable psychedelic effects, which served as a placebo, and then a 25-milligram high dose known to induce a profound altered state of consciousness.
